cues.text: Scammers register lookalikes of NEAR accounts and dApp domains. Wallets and agents can't tell them apart.
Mimicwatch generated 33 thousand lookalikes of 72 official accounts of 34 NEAR dApps and asked mainnet which exist: 507 do.
Each one is scored from on-chain facts: age, creator, keys, contracts, tokens, and who sent it money.
Three are fake reward tokens. linear_protocol.near advertises a phishing site and sits in 2,205 wallets. One of the three created the other two.
Not every lookalike is a scam: someone's own account, a brand's defensive name. These are labelled, and never published.
The domain scan adds 53 lookalike domains, including a fresh clone of the Rhea app that asks for seed phrases.
Everything lands in a review queue. Nothing publishes itself: only findings a reviewer approved, at high or critical, go on chain.
The publisher writes them to the registry contract, here on a local NEAR node, with the hash of each evidence file.
Now an agent is told to pay. Before it signs, it asks the registry.
Pay 25 NEAR to linear_protocol.near? Blocked, with a link to the evidence.
A sub-account of a flagged account is blocked too: only the parent can create it.
The real LiNEAR contract is allowed.
A lookalike nobody has reviewed yet gets a warning, so a human decides.
And the Rhea clone is blocked as a link.
If an entry is wrong, anyone can dispute it on chain with a small deposit. While it is disputed, wallets warn instead of blocking.
The owner reviews the dispute and keeps the entry, so it blocks again. Accepting it would clear the entry and refund the deposit.
The same contract is live on NEAR testnet, with an MCP tool for agents. What should your wallet check before it sends?
